segments.say: Lesson 13. Tool Calling & ReAct Agents. How an L L M "uses tools": function schemas, the agent loop, ReAct, and when to use a workflow instead of an agent.

An A I agent is an L L M that can use tools (call A P Is, run queries) in a loop: think leads to act leads to observe the result leads to think again, until the task is done. Here is an analogy. A manager who can't touch a keyboard: they write instructions on sticky notes ("check C P U on prod-1"), an assistant runs them and reports back, and the manager decides the next step.

Why does this matter? Agents are the centre of current A I engineering (F D E, A I ops, automation roles). Tool calling is how L L Ms connect to real systems. A few key words. Tool / function: An action the model may request, described by a jason schema. Tool call: The model's structured request: name plus arguments. Observation: The tool's result, fed back to the model. ReAct: Reason plus Act loop. Workflow versus agent: Steps fixed in code versus decided by the L L M.
Chatbot versus agent. A plain chatbot can only produce text. It can explain how to restart a job, but you still have to do it.
An agent is given tools, functions it may ask your code to run.
It calls check job(), reads the result, decides to call restart job(), verifies, and reports back. Model plus tools plus a loop equals agent. The next scene shows that loop in detail.
The agent loop (ReAct). The user's request needs live data plus an action. The L L M alone can do neither.
You send the message plus tool schemas (name, description, jason parameters). The L L M thinks: "I need C P U data first."
The L L M doesn't execute anything. It returns a structured tool call: "name":"get cpu","args": "host":"prod-1". Your code runs it.
Your runtime calls the real A P I (validated, authorized, with a timeout).
The result goes back to the L L M as an observation: "C P U 94% for 15 min".
The L L M reasons again: "That's high, so create a ticket", and emits a second tool call.
When no more tools are needed it writes the final answer. Thought leads to Action leads to Observation, repeated: that's ReAct.

Tool / function calling. You describe tools as jason schemas with great names and descriptions. The description is a prompt. The model returns which tool to call plus arguments. Your code executes it and returns the result. Models can request parallel tool calls when the calls are independent. Always validate arguments (Pydantic), enforce auth, set timeouts, and handle errors by returning them as observations so the model can recover.

Workflows versus agents. Workflow: you define the steps in code (prompt chaining, routing, parallelization, orchestrator-workers, evaluator-optimizer). Predictable, testable, cheaper. Agent: the L L M decides the steps dynamically in a loop. Flexible for open-ended tasks, but less predictable. Rule of thumb: use the simplest thing that works. Many "agents" in production are really workflows with one or two L L M decisions.

Making agents reliable. Cap iterations and token budget. Detect loops. Keep tool count small and descriptions distinct, since too many similar tools confuse selection. Human-in-the-loop approval for destructive actions (delete, deploy, pay). Least-privilege credentials per tool. Trace every step (Lang Smith) and evaluate tool-selection accuracy.

Analogy. The L L M is a manager who can't touch a keyboard. It writes instructions on sticky notes ("call get cpu on prod-1"). An intern (your code) runs them and reports back. The manager decides the next note.

Say it in the interview. "In tool calling the model only proposes structured calls. My runtime validates and executes them with least privilege, timeouts and error handling, then feeds results back as observations. That's the ReAct loop. I prefer deterministic workflows where the steps are known and use agents only for genuinely open-ended tasks, with iteration caps, human approval for risky actions and full tracing.".

Let's compare. Prompt chain: your code, high, extract leads to validate leads to summarize. Router: L L M picks a branch once, high, billing versus tech support. Parallelization: your code, high, check 5 policies at once, then vote. Orchestrator-workers: L L M splits task, workers do parts, medium, multi-file code change. Evaluator-optimizer: L L M generates, another critiques, loop, medium, translation refinement. Autonomous agent: L L M in a loop with tools, low, open-ended incident investigation.

A likely interview question: Agent versus workflow? A strong answer: A workflow has code-defined steps: predictable and cheap. An agent is an L L M deciding steps in a loop with tools: flexible but costlier and less predictable. Pick the simplest that meets requirements.
That's it for Tool Calling & ReAct Agents. Now play the quiz and games in the app to lock it in. See you in the next lesson.
